Date/Time: 2026-12-15 16:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees (Redwood): Nora Patel (AE), Marcus Lee (SE), Jules Romero (Solutions)
Attendees (Customer): Samir Gupta (Eng Mgr), Hannah Cho (Lead ML Eng), Maya Rivera (Product), plus an engineer on audio (Speaker 3)

transcript:
[00:00] Nora (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intros — I'm Nora, AE on the hosted API team. Marcus, do you want to say hi?
[00:08] Marcus (Redwood SE): Yeah hi, Marcus here. I'll run the live bits — console, a quick sample curl and then a tiny perf sketch.
[00:14] Samir (Arbor): Samir — thanks. We're mainly focused on chat experiences in store ops — low latency, sometimes on flaky mobile, so retry behavior is big for us.
[00:22] Nora: Great, that's exactly what we'll show. Quick agenda: streaming fundamentals, key params, retry/backoff, then console + Optimize hints and next steps.
[00:35] Hannah (Arbor): Quick note: security is on the call list later, but we might interrupt with SOC2/KMS questions.
[00:40] Nora: Totally — we'll cover the basics and then we can slot a short security Q&A.
[01:02] Marcus: Alright I'm sharing the console. First thing — when you call the chatgen endpoint with streaming enabled you get delta frames chunked as they arrive, so the client can render partial tokens. We send event chunks with a small metadata prefix.
[01:30] Speaker 3: sorry, can you show the raw stream?
[01:33] Marcus: Yes — here's a live curl with --no-buffer. You'll see server-sent events where each chunk contains the token text and sometimes the role. Example payload: data: {"type":"delta","display_text":"Hello"} — it's slightly different across SDKs but the concept's same.
[02:05] Samir: How big are the chunks — is it per-token, or grouped?
[02:09] Marcus: Good question. It's not necessarily one token per chunk — it depends on generation throughput and batching. The runtime groups tokens and flushes them frequently. In practice you see 4-30 char chunks for English. If you do high-temp exploration it can be a bit more bursty.
[02:35] Hannah: Does that affect latency SLA? If you get grouped tokens, does average first-byte latency increase?
[02:40] Marcus: The first-byte latency is typically stable — it's the time to first commit which we try to keep low. Grouping affects the smoothness of streaming rather than the initial response time. If you need super-smooth single-token updates, there are SDK knobs to prefer smaller flushes at a slight cost.
[03:11] Nora: Let's talk params — quick hit: max_tokens sets the output ceiling, temperature controls randomness, top_p controls nucleus sampling, and n controls multiple completions. For chat flows we usually recommend temperature 0.0-0.6 for deterministic UX, or 0.7+ for creative flows.
[03:40] Maya (Arbor): For our use case — suggested defaults? low-latency help chat.
[03:45] Marcus: For help chat, temp 0.0-0.3, top_p 0.8-1.0, max_tokens 80-200 depending on your typical reply length. Also stop sequences are useful to avoid trailing boilerplate.
[04:08] Samir: On retries — we have flaky mobile. What's your recommended pattern? exponential backoff?
[04:13] Marcus: We recommend idempotency where possible. For chat generation we expose a request_id header — if you send the same request_id and the backend has a cached response we can return the cached stream. For intermittent network fails, do a short immediate reconnect and then exponential backoff for repeated failures. Also make sure your client is deduping on message ids.
[04:45] Hannah: Is the request_id the same as conversation id or something separate?
[04:49] Marcus: We separate them. Conversation id groups messages; request_id is per-API call for idempotency. If you reissue the same request_id we can return the same token sequence.
[05:06] Samir: What about partial responses? If the client disconnects mid-stream, can we resume?
[05:11] Marcus: We don't have fine-grained byte-range resume today — resume is at RPC level: you can re-run with the same request_id and get the full (or cached) output. For long-form generation we recommend smaller checkpoints — e.g., chunking prompts so you have meaningful atomic units. Also KV caching on the runtime reduces cost for repeated prefixes.
[05:38] Nora: Quick Optimize tip — for repetitive flows we suggest prefix caching and lower precision quantized variants for cost savings, Optimize will surface suggestions in the console based on token distributions.
[05:58] Speaker 3: quantized variants — can you explain the quality tradeoff?
[06:02] Marcus: Sure. 8-bit quant tends to be very good for many open models; you may see minor quality regressions in edge cases. Optimize can run a quality regression check on a small eval set and recommend keep or roll back.
[06:27] Maya: We have question on dedicated vs hosted — Architect tells us they want predictable p99 latency under 300ms. Can hosted hit that?
[06:35] Nora: Hosted can hit tight p50/p90 for many configs. For strict p99 under 300ms we usually recommend Dedicated pools — those give you reserved GPU capacity and deterministic scheduling. But there are cost tradeoffs — hosted with smart routing and burst reservations can still be a good middle ground.
[06:58] Hannah: Any example numbers?
[07:02] Marcus: On a standard gen model we published benchmarks for 16k context and single-stream latency: median ~80-120ms, p95 ~220-320ms depending on sequence length. For p99 under 300 we recommend dedicated or model+quant combo and limiting max_tokens. We'll include a benchmarking sheet.
[07:28] Samir: Security: do you support customer-managed KMS and audit logs?
[07:33] Nora: Yes — for Private deployments you can bring your own KMS/HSM, and even for Dedicated we support customer-managed keys and audit logging. Hosted API retains logs for troubleshooting but we can configure retention or purge per contract. We'll send the SOC2 summary and a security checklist.
[08:01] Marcus: Quick demo: I'm switching to live curl that streams with SSE. I'll trigger a couple of requests with different temps so you see the difference in chunking.
[08:15] [Marcus runs two sample calls visible in console, one temp=0.1, one temp=0.9]
[08:25] Marcus: See how temp=0.1 gives conservative completions and more predictable token flow; temp=0.9 is more bursty and you may see bigger chunks as the generator explores.
[08:45] Hannah: Can backpressure from client lead to server-side queueing? If our client is slow, do you buffer?
[08:50] Marcus: We have per-connection buffers; if the client is slow we eventually drop the connection on extreme cases but typical behavior is the runtime will batch other requests and not block the generator — you'll see slightly larger chunk sizes for the slow connection. For guaranteed low-latency UX we recommend client-side streaming readers that read promptly and flow-control on sockets.
[09:18] Samir: We do websockets for mobile. Does Redwood have a websocket SDK?
[09:22] Nora: We have official SDKs for web and Node, plus websocket patterns in the docs. If you need a polished mobile example we can share a small sample repo.
[09:35] Speaker 3: how do retries interact with billing? If we reissue request do we pay twice?
[09:40] Marcus: Billing is per token generated. If you reissue with the same request_id and the runtime returns a cached response, you won't be billed again for the same tokens — caching helps there. If it's a fresh run, you'll be billed for tokens generated. Optimize helps by recommending caching where it detects repeated prefixes.
[10:06] Maya: In our flows we sometimes do short follow-up edits — is editing supported?
[10:11] Marcus: We have chat edit patterns: you can send an incremental prompt with context; the KV cache and prefix cache make that cheap. For heavy edits we recommend re-anchoring prompts so you avoid long recomputation.
[10:33] Nora: Ok quick pause — any blocker-level questions?
[10:36] Hannah: We need to know p99 numbers with our sample prompt lengths and expected concurrency. Also a security contact.
[10:42] Nora: Noted — Marcus will run a perf test; I'll send pricing and security docs.
[10:48] Marcus: Now a small note on idempotency tokens and safe retry semantics — we recommend an Idempotency header plus a client-side request checksum for payloads with attachments. For streaming we also surface chunk checksums in logs to help debug incomplete streams; sometimes the transcript will show garbled words (transcription can be imperfect).
[11:18] Samir: Could you show the Console token breakdown?
[11:21] Marcus: Showing it now — you can see tokens per request, cost estimate, and a waterfall for prefix vs generated tokens. There's also a latency histogram and a per-route breakdown.
[11:45] Marcus: The Optimize tab flagged this route as "high prefix reuse" — we'd suggest enabling prefix cache and adjusting batching window from 100ms to 60ms to hit better throughput without hurting first-byte latency.
[12:03] Maya: That sounds useful — can Optimize produce a one-click toggle?
[12:06] Marcus: Not one-click to change infra, but Optimize will create suggested config snippets and you can export them to your infra-as-code or apply via the console if you have proper RBAC.
[12:26] Hannah: Any notes on regional routing? We need EU data residency for some flows.
[12:31] Nora: Yes — you can pin routes to regions and we support regional model catalogs. For strict residency we suggest Private or Dedicated in your region. We'll include region-specific docs.
[12:48] Samir: About support SLAs?
[12:52] Nora: We have standardized SLA tiers; Dedicated customers get shorter incident response and a named technical account manager. Hosted has standard response windows. Pricing doc will outline tiers.
[13:10] Marcus: Quick demo wrap-up — I ran the benchmark sketch earlier in the sandbox: 50 concurrent simulated clients, avg 120 tokens per request, median latency 110ms, p95 260ms. I'll reproduce this against Arbor sample prompts and share the CSV.
[13:36] Maya: Great. Anything on cost optimization besides caching and quant?
[13:40] Marcus: Also consider batching small requests into micro-batches at the client side if you can tolerate a 50-100ms batching window. For stateless short replies it's often a huge unit-cost win.
[13:58] Samir: Last topic — procurement. We might need to include security attestation docs in our RFP.
[14:05] Nora: We'll attach SOC2, pen test summary, and the KMS/retention checklist to the follow-up email.
[14:20] Speaker 3: small nit — sometimes the SDK doc mentions KV "cash" instead of cache, saw that in a different export — just FYI.
[14:27] Marcus: Ha, yes typo. We'll fix docs.
[14:33] Nora: Okay let's recap next steps: pricing + burst policy, perf benchmark, security deep dive scheduling. Anything else?
[14:40] Maya: Can we get a short mobile example for websockets?
[14:43] Nora: Yes — I'll add a sample mobile websocket repo link.
[14:48] Samir: Thanks all.
[14:50] Marcus: One last note — if you start a pilot we can provide a limited Dedicated pilot window for critical routes to validate p99.
[14:59] Nora: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with the items.
[15:05] [Meeting ends]

Notes about transcription quality: occasional mislabels (Speaker 3), small typos in docs referenced, and a few words mis-transcribed (e.g., "KV cash" vs "KV cache"). The recording aligns with the 48 minute duration though this exported snippet is compressed for brevity.
